questions.q: In the lecturer's discussion of the diagnostic classifier, what does accuracy mean?
options: The standard assay for measuring the amount of a particular protein in a liquid sample.
A chip carrying thousands of gene probes, used to measure which genes are switched on.
The proportion of diagnostic test calls that are correct, that is, the overall performance obtained by weighting sensitivity and specificity.
The study of the whole proteome, used to find biomarkers and targets.
questions.why: The figures the lecturer gives for the classifier are AUC 0.981, sensitivity 98.25%, specificity 91.53% and accuracy 94.83%; together these four numbers give a complete description of how good the classifier is. When reading them you have to keep the denominators apart: of 100 people without HCC, about 91-92 are correctly called negative, which is what specificity measures, whereas of 100 people with HCC, 98 are correctly called positive, which is what sensitivity measures; accuracy is the proportion of diagnostic test calls that are correct, that is, the overall performance obtained by weighting sensitivity and specificity. If a question asks how many of 100 healthy people would be falsely flagged, you have to calculate it with specificity.

questions.q: In Lect 1 the lecturer splits biomarkers into three uses; which of the following statements most correctly captures the difference between a prognostic biomarker and a predictive biomarker?
options: A prognostic biomarker answers 'how will the disease turn out', whereas a predictive biomarker answers 'will this drug work for this patient'.
It tells you whether the patient has the disease right now.
The study of the whole proteome, used to find biomarkers and targets.
A chip carrying thousands of gene probes, used to measure which genes are switched on.
questions.why: In Lect 1 the lecturer divides biomarkers into three uses - diagnostic, prognostic and predictive - and this classification is one of the main threads running through his whole course. Diagnostic answers 'is the patient ill now' (for example SEPT9 methylation for colorectal cancer screening); prognostic answers 'how will the disease turn out' (for example ERBB2 being favourable in renal cancer but unfavourable in pancreatic cancer); predictive answers 'will this drug work for this patient' (for example cetuximab being ineffective in rectal cancer with a K-Ras mutation). He specifically lists the prognostic and predictive pair as a distractor pair, so you have to be able to tell them apart.

questions.q: What is the English name for the type of test that has to be done before treatment in order to decide whether a patient can be given that drug?
options: FISH
Diagnostic biomarker
Specificity
Companion diagnostic
questions.why: The lecturer describes a companion diagnostic as binding 'drug treatment' and 'testing' into a single decision: HER2 amplification is read out by FISH (HER2/CEP17 ratio ≥ 2.0 or HER2 copy number ≥ 6), and the result decides whether the patient is suitable for Herceptin; conversely, rectal cancer with a K-Ras mutation should not receive cetuximab even if HER2 is normal. In practice it is the product of developing the drug registration and the test in parallel - without a matched companion test there is no way to decide who should get the drug; by contrast, a marker such as CEA, which tracks tumour burden, is a surrogate marker.

questions.q: The lecturer splits biomarkers into three uses - diagnostic, prognostic and predictive; the one that answers 'does the patient actually have the disease right now' and is used for screening and confirmation is called ____.
options: Companion diagnostic
Diagnostic biomarker
Sensitivity
Specificity
questions.why: In Lect 3 the lecturer sorts the usable tests by sampling site and use: stool-based early screening uses ITG4, SFRP2 methylation, Cologuard, miR-21, miR-92a and miR-135b; blood-based early screening uses SEPT9 methylation, SFRP2 methylation, miR-21, miR-92a and miR-29a. Clinically there is a trade-off between sensitivity and specificity: a false positive brings unnecessary follow-up investigations, whereas a false negative misses a patient who could have been treated. The boundary between diagnostic on the one hand and prognostic and predictive on the other is one of the distractor pairs the lecturer lists.

questions.q: What role does ELISA play in the lecturer's biomarker workflow?
options: A test that uses DNA probes rather than antibodies to count gene copies inside cells (for example HER2).
A chip carrying thousands of gene probes, used to measure which genes are switched on.
The standard assay for measuring the amount of a particular protein in a liquid sample.
The study of the whole proteome, used to find biomarkers and targets.
questions.why: ELISA stands for enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay: a pair of specific antibodies sandwiches the target protein in the sample, one antibody immobilised on the plate and the other carrying an enzyme label; after the unbound material is washed away, substrate is added and the enzyme generates the colour, whose intensity is proportional to the amount of target protein. In the HCC case this is the final and most crucial step: the vimentin signal originally found on the 2D-PAGE was moved into serum and quantified by ELISA, becoming a biomarker that patients can have measured from a blood sample. The figures the lecturer gives are serum vimentin in controls 176.0 ± 61.3 ng/mL, HCC ≤ 2 cm 271.5 ± 165.9 and HCC > 2 cm 231.3 ± 132.3.

questions.q: What is the English name for the type of test that uses DNA probes rather than antibodies to count gene copies inside cells (for example HER2)?
options: FISH
ELISA
Western blot
qPCR
questions.why: The lecturer points out that FISH uses fluorescently labelled DNA probes, which hybridise with complementary DNA sequences inside the cell, and a fluorescence microscope is then used to see where the signal falls, so gene copy number can be counted with DNA probes rather than antibodies. FISH for HER2 uses two probes: the HER2/NEU probe marks 17q12 and the CEP17 centromeric probe marks 17p11.1, and the interpretation criteria are a HER2/CEP17 ratio ≥ 2.0 or a HER2 copy number ≥ 6. He also states plainly that experimental parameters such as the denaturation temperature will not be examined, but the contrast 'DNA probes rather than antibodies, which is therefore how gene copy number can be counted' is worth remembering.

questions.q: The lecturer demonstrated this mechanism in Lect 2: the instrument uses a fast-moving liquid to squeeze the sample stream from the centre into an extremely thin thread, so that cells can only pass through the laser one at a time in single file. This fluid-dynamics technique is called ____.
options: sheath fluid
Isoelectric focusing
Western blot
hydrodynamic focusing
questions.why: The instrument uses a fast-moving liquid called sheath fluid to squeeze the sample stream from the centre into an extremely thin thread, so that cells can only pass through the laser one at a time in single file. This is exactly why flow cytometry counts accurately: if two cells pass together their scatter signals overlap and cannot be told apart; if the focus is lost the signals interfere with one another and the count becomes unreliable, so this is the physical basis of flow cytometry's quantitative capability.

questions.q: 2D-PAGE separates proteins in two dimensions; which method is used for the dimension that separates them by charge?
options: A chip carrying thousands of gene probes, used to measure which genes are switched on.
A method that separates proteins according to the pH at which they carry no net charge.
A test that uses DNA probes rather than antibodies to count gene copies inside cells (for example HER2).
The standard assay for measuring the amount of a particular protein in a liquid sample.
questions.why: Every protein has a specific pH at which its total charge is zero (the isoelectric point, pI). The sample is placed on a strip of pH-gradient gel (for example 4.0 to 9.0) and an electric field is applied, so the proteins migrate in the direction that brings their own net charge to zero and finally come to rest at their pI; proteins with the same pI therefore stack on the same band, giving high resolution. It cannot separate proteins of similar molecular weight, so in the lecturer's 2D-PAGE IEF forms the charge-based dimension and SDS-PAGE the molecular-weight-based dimension (220 kDa down to 10 kDa), after which the spots are cut out and identified by LC-MS/MS.

questions.q: What is the English name for the technique that uses a chip carrying thousands of gene probes to measure which genes are switched on?
options: RNA sequencing
Proteomics
Microarray
Isoelectric focusing
questions.why: The lecturer introduces two ways of doing a microarray: the oligonucleotide GeneChip converts the sample's mRNA into biotin-labelled cRNA and is stained in a single colour, whereas the cDNA microarray labels normal and tumour tissue with two different fluorochromes, Cy5 and Cy3, mixes them and then performs competitive hybridisation on the chip; wherever the signal at a position leans towards one colour, that gene is more strongly expressed in that group. His miRNA biomarker workflow is a three-stage validation - 'tumour versus adjacent tissue, then cell-line supernatant, then patient serum before and after surgery' - and the whole-cohort comparison stage uses tools of this kind; he also reminds us that adjacent tissue is not the same as normal tissue.

questions.q: When a flow cytometer is used to analyse the cell cycle, which dye is used to stain DNA so that the DNA content of each cell can be measured?
options: A dye that stains DNA, so that entering the flow cytometer tells you how much DNA each cell contains.
The fluid stream in a flow cytometer that squeezes the sample stream into a single thread.
A method that separates proteins according to the pH at which they carry no net charge.
Quantitative PCR, which uses a fluorescent signal to measure how much of a given DNA segment is present in a sample.
questions.why: PI intercalates between the bases of DNA, so the fluorescence intensity is proportional to the DNA content. It cannot cross an intact cell membrane, so the cells have to be fixed and permeabilised before staining. The resulting histogram has two peaks: G1 is 2N, S phase is the continuous rise between the two peaks, and G2/M is 4N. This is the quickest way of resolving the cell cycle, and it is also the measurement tool the lecturer uses when studying DNA replication, where the DNA content is 1 before replication and 2 after. The lecturer places it on the tiered list of flow cytometry basics; the companion figure is reducing FBS to 0.5–1% for serum starvation so that the cells arrest at G1 in synchrony.

questions.q: In Lect 1 the lecturer uses proteomics to show how the biomarker vimentin was found; which of the following statements most aptly describes the role of proteomics in that workflow?
options: The standard assay for measuring the amount of a particular protein in a liquid sample.
A test that uses DNA probes rather than antibodies to count gene copies inside cells (for example HER2).
A chip carrying thousands of gene probes, used to measure which genes are switched on.

First separate by charge with isoelectric focusing and then by molecular weight with SDS-PAGE to obtain a map of spots, cut the spots out and digest them, then read out the peptides with LC-MS/MS and identify their identity against a database.
questions.why: The lecturer's proteomics workflow is 2D-PAGE plus LC-MS/MS, and he warns about an easy mistake: the adjacent tissue next to a tumour is not biochemically the same as genuinely normal tissue, so it should not be used as the 'healthy group' for comparison, and this step decides the credibility of the whole biomarker paper. He also states plainly that the pharmaceutical industry's target nomination and druggability workflow will not be examined - do not memorise the procedure, understand the concepts: taking a spot map all the way to a marker that can be tested in blood is the point of this workflow.

questions.q: Both of the lecturer's two biomarker worklines rely on it for validation: the hepatocellular carcinoma line uses it to validate the vimentin found by 2D-PAGE, while the Lect 4 line uses it to check whether the anti-TERT antisense oligonucleotide really drives down TERT mRNA. Which method does this refer to?
options: The technology that reads all the RNA in a sample as sequences.
Quantitative PCR, which uses a fluorescent signal to measure how much of a given DNA segment is present in a sample.
The standard protein assay for seeing whether a particular protein is present in a sample.
A dye that stains DNA, so that entering the flow cytometer tells you how much DNA each cell contains.
questions.why: Ordinary PCR only answers 'is it there or not', whereas qPCR also answers 'how much': the product doubles in every cycle and the fluorescent signal accumulates, and the instrument back-calculates the starting template amount from the cycle at which the fluorescence reaches threshold, so the less target there is in the sample the more cycles are needed. It is far more sensitive than plain PCR, which is why it became the validation tool on both of the lecturer's biomarker worklines. The figure he asks you to remember comes from the TERT experiment: 3 weeks of anti-TERT pretreatment gave a tumour formation rate of 2/12 (9/12 in untreated), Fisher's p = 0.01.

questions.q: The lecturer points out that a microarray can only ask 'are these genes I specified present?', whereas ____ shows both 'which genes are expressed' and 'how much they are expressed', needs no genes to be specified in advance, and is irreplaceable for discovering new transcripts.
options: Microarray
Proteomics
RNA sequencing
qPCR
questions.why: The RNA sequencing workflow is: extract the RNA, fragment it, use reverse transcriptase to convert each fragment into DNA, add adapter fragments, build a DNA library, and then have the machine read out the sequences and align them to the genome. Its value lies in showing both 'which genes are expressed' and 'how much they are expressed', whereas a microarray can only ask 'are these genes I specified present?'; its cost and the analytical threshold it demands are higher than for a microarray, but because no genes need to be specified in advance it is irreplaceable for discovering new transcripts. The lecturer does not name it as an examination topic in its own right - it is a matter of understanding the concept, with the emphasis on the omics workflow.

questions.q: What is the English name for the index that says what proportion of genuinely diseased patients are correctly picked out by the test?
options: Sensitivity
Specificity
accuracy
Companion diagnostic
questions.why: The denominator for sensitivity is all the people who really are ill: if the test calls 98 of 100 true patients positive, the sensitivity is 98%. It answers the question 'how many patients does this test miss?', and the missed patients are the false negatives, the group whose treatment is delayed. Conversely, the denominator for specificity is all the people who really are well, and it answers 'will healthy people be misjudged as patients?'. The lecturer's miRNA classifier figures are sensitivity 98.25%, specificity 91.53% and accuracy 94.83%; these four numbers are the language in which an ROC curve is read.

questions.q: In a flow cytometer, what is the fast-moving fluid stream that squeezes the sample stream from the centre into an extremely thin thread, so that cells can only pass through the laser one at a time?
options: The fluid-dynamics technique that makes cells pass through the laser beam in single file.
A dye that stains DNA, so that entering the flow cytometer tells you how much DNA each cell contains.
A method that separates proteins according to the pH at which they carry no net charge.
The fluid stream in a flow cytometer that squeezes the sample stream into a single thread.
questions.why: The instrument injects a fast-moving sheath fluid from the side, which squeezes the central sample stream and flattens it to an extreme thinness, so that cells can only pass through the laser one at a time. Without this trick, two cells passing together would produce overlapping signals and the count would immediately go out of step. The ratio of the sheath flow rate to the sample flow rate determines the degree of focusing, and it is the parameter that is adjusted most often on the instrument. The lecturer covers sheath fluid and hydrodynamic focusing in the same segment; it is a matter of understanding the concept.

questions.q: In Lect 1 the lecturer uses a set of figures to teach students how to read an ROC curve; which of the following statements most correctly captures the difference between specificity and sensitivity, that complementary pair of indices?
options: The study of the whole proteome, used to find biomarkers and targets.

The denominator for specificity is all the people who really are well, and it answers whether healthy people will be misjudged as patients; the denominator for sensitivity is the people who really are ill, and it answers whether patients will be missed.
A chip carrying thousands of gene probes, used to measure which genes are switched on.
A test that has to be done before treatment in order to decide whether a patient can be given that drug.
questions.why: The denominator for specificity is all the people who really are well. If the test calls 92 of 100 healthy people negative, the specificity is 92%; the remaining 8 judged positive are false positives, and they bring unnecessary biopsies, further tests and anxiety. It is a complementary mirror of sensitivity: the former governs 'will healthy people be turned into patients', the latter governs 'will patients be missed'. The clinical trade-off is that screening uses high sensitivity to keep the room for missed diagnoses small, while confirmation uses high specificity to reduce harm done in error. The figure the lecturer gives is a specificity of 91.53% for the miR-15b plus miR-130b classifier, and the AUC of the same classifier is 0.981.

questions.q: In the vimentin case in Lect 1 the lecturer treats it as one of the validation tools (alongside qPCR, IHC and ELISA), and on the codon-optimisation slide he uses it to compare target protein expression across different treatment groups. Which detection method does this refer to?
options: A dye that stains DNA, so that entering the flow cytometer tells you how much DNA each cell contains.
The technology that reads all the RNA in a sample as sequences.
The standard protein assay for seeing whether a particular protein is present in a sample.
The study of the whole proteome, used to find biomarkers and targets.
questions.why: The Western blot workflow is: use SDS-PAGE to separate the proteins by size, then 'transfer' the proteins from the gel onto a membrane; an antibody binds the target protein and a labelled second antibody detects it. Seeing a band means the protein is present in the sample, and the depth of the band indicates how much. Its strength is answering 'is it there' and 'how much', and its weakness is that it cannot reveal the whole proteome in a single run. The lecturer does not list it as an examination topic; all you need is to say that it answers 'is it there / how much', and to keep clear how it divides labour with SDS-PAGE, LC-MS/MS and X-ray.
